(p-244) The Exalted said: ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: on Sunday and Monday. This was also the view of 'Abdullah ibn Salam, al-Suddi, and most scholars. Muqatil said: on Tuesday and Wednesday. Muslim, in his *Afrad* (the narrations he related alone), recorded from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took my hand and said: 'Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created the clay on Saturday, created the mountains in it on Sunday, created the trees in it on Monday, created the disliked things on Tuesday, created the light on Wednesday, and dispersed the creatures in it on Thursday.'" This hadith contradicts what preceded it, and it is more authentic.

The Exalted said: ﴿And you set up rivals to Him﴾. We have explained this in [Al-Baqarah: 22]. ﴿That﴾, the One who did what was mentioned, is ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾.

﴿And He placed in it firm mountains﴾, meaning mountains fixed firmly above the earth. ﴿And He blessed it﴾ with trees, fruits, grains, and rivers. It was also said: its blessing is that it makes the crops grow, so that one grain produces many grains and one date-stone produces a palm tree. ﴿And He measured in it its sustenance﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *aqwat* is the plural of *qut*, which means provisions and what is needed.

The exegetes have five opinions regarding this measuring:

First: He split the rivers and planted the trees. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: He apportioned the provisions of the servants and the animals. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: Its sustenance is from the rain. This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: He decreed for each land what He did not give to another, just as the garments of Yemen are not suitable except in Yemen, and the Harawiyyah (cloths) are only made in Herat, so that some of them might live off others through trade. This was said by 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

Fifth: He decreed wheat for the people of one region, dates for the people of another region, and millet for the people of another region. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The Exalted said: ﴿in four days﴾, meaning in full four days. Al-Akhfash said: the likeness of this is when you say: "I married a woman yesterday, and two today, and one of them is the one I married yesterday."

The exegetes said: that is, Tuesday and Wednesday, and together with Sunday and Monday these make four days.

(p-245) The Exalted said: ﴿equally﴾. Abu Ja'far read it *sawa'un* with a *damma*. Ya'qub and 'Abd al-Warith read it *sawa'in* with a *kasra*. The rest of the ten (canonical reciters) read it with a *fatha*. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it with a *kasra* makes *sawa'an* a description of the days, so the meaning is: in four days that are equal and complete. Whoever reads it with a *fatha* takes it as a verbal noun, so the meaning is: they were equal, with equality. Whoever reads it with a *damma* takes it to mean: it is equal.

Regarding the Exalted's words ﴿for those who ask﴾ there are two possibilities. One: for those who ask about sustenance, since everyone seeks sustenance and asks for it. Two: for whoever asks: "In how many days was the earth created?" It is said: it was created in four equal days, with no addition or subtraction.

The Exalted said: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾. We have explained this in [Al-Baqarah: 29]. ﴿And it was smoke﴾, and regarding this there are two opinions:

One: when He created the water, He sent wind over it, and smoke rose from it, ascended, and rose high, so He named it "sky" (*sama'*).

The second: when He created the earth, He sent fire upon it, and smoke rose from it and rose high.

The Exalted said: ﴿And He said to it and to the earth﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He said to the heaven: "Make your sun, your moon, and your stars appear," and He said to the earth: "Split open your rivers and bring forth your fruits." ﴿Come willingly or unwillingly.﴾ They both said: ﴿We come willingly.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). The reason it did not say *ta'i'at* (feminine plural) is that they were treated as beings that understand and discern, as He said about the stars: ﴿and each in an orbit swims along﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40]. He said: it has also been said: "We and those with us came willingly."

﴿Then He completed them﴾, meaning He created them and fashioned them. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said: (p-246)

"Upon them both are two coats of mail, woven by Dawud, or made by the artisans of Tubba'."

Its meaning: he made them and fashioned them.

The Exalted said: ﴿in two days﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: they are Thursday and Friday. Muqatil said: Sunday and Monday, because his view is that the heaven was created before the earth. We have explained the length of these days in [Al-A'raf: 54].

﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. One: He revealed what He willed and commanded what He wished. This was said by Mujahid and Muqatil. The second: He created in each heaven its creation. This was said by al-Suddi.

The Exalted said: ﴿And We adorned the nearest heaven﴾, that is, the heaven nearest to the earth, ﴿with lamps﴾, which are the stars. The word *masabih* means lamps, and a star is called a *misbah* because of its shining. ﴿And as protection﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: We protected it from the eavesdropping of the devils by means of the stars, as a protection.

The exegetes said: they mean Iblis and Qabil, because they both initiated disobedience. ﴿That we may put them under our feet so they will be among the lowest﴾, meaning in the lowest level (darak, the lowest level of the Fire), which is more severe in punishment than the others.

(p-254) The first: they remained steadfast upon monotheism (tawhid). This was said by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Mujahid.

The second: they remained steadfast upon obedience to Allah and the performance of His obligations. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The third: they remained steadfast upon sincerity and action until death. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Suddi.

'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, because the polytheists said, "Our Lord is Allah, and the angels are His daughters, and these are our intercessors with Allah," so they did not remain steadfast. The Jews said, "Our Lord is Allah, and 'Uzayr is His son, and Muhammad is not a prophet," so they did not remain steadfast. The Christians said, "Our Lord is Allah, and the Messiah is His son, and Muhammad is not a prophet," so they did not remain steadfast. And Abu Bakr said, "Our Lord is Allah alone, and Muhammad is His servant and messenger," and so he remained steadfast.

The first: do not fear death, and do not grieve over your children, said by Mujahid. The second: do not fear what is before you, and do not grieve over what is behind you, said by 'Ikrimah and al-Suddi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 41, verse 33–36:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah﴾. There are three opinions regarding who is meant by this.

The first: they are the muezzins (the callers to prayer). Jabir ibn Abdullah narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "It was revealed concerning the muezzins." This is also the view of Aisha, Mujahid, and Ikrimah.

The second: it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who invited to the testimony that there is no god but Allah. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

The third: it is the believer who answered Allah in what He called him to, and called people to that, ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ in his answering. This was said by al-Hasan.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: he prayed two rak'ahs after the adhan. This is the view of Aisha and Mujahid. Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated from Qays ibn Abi Hazim: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah﴾, he said: the adhan. ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, he said: the prayer between the adhan and the iqamah.

The second: he performed the obligatory duties and upheld the rights of Allah. This was said by Ata.

The third: he fasted and prayed. This was said by Ikrimah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Good and evil are not equal﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "la" (not) is an emphatic additional particle; the meaning is: good and evil are not equal. The exegetes have three opinions regarding these two terms.

The first: the good deed is faith, and the evil deed is polytheism. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: the good is forbearance (hilm), and the evil is foul speech (fuhsh). This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: the good is aversion (to evil) and patience. This was related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾. This is like repelling anger with patience, and offense with pardon. When you do that, the one between you and whom there is enmity becomes like a close friend. Ata said: it is greeting with peace the one you are at odds with when you meet him. The exegetes said: this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But none is granted it﴾, i.e., none is given it. Al-Zajjaj said: none is granted this act, which is repelling an evil deed with a good one, ﴿except those who are patient﴾ in restraining anger, ﴿and none is granted it except one of great fortune﴾ in goodness. Al-Suddi said: except one of great fortune (jadd). Qatadah said: the great fortune is Paradise; so the meaning is: none is granted it except the one for whom Paradise is obligatory.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should tempt you﴾. We have explained it in [al-A'raf: 200].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 41, verse 40–42:

(p-261) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our verses﴾. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. We have already explained the meaning of ilhad (deviation, distortion) in [an-Nahl: 103]. Regarding what is meant by it here there are five opinions.

The first: that he placed speech other than in its proper place. Al-Awfi narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is whistling and clapping during the recitation of the Qur'an. Mujahid said this.

The third: that it is denial of the verses. Qatadah said this.

The fourth: that it is obstinate opposition. As-Suddi said this.

The fifth: that it is turning away from belief in the verses. Muqatil said this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are not hidden from Us.﴾ This is a warning of recompense. ﴿Is he who is thrown into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ This is general, except that the exegetes have mentioned seven opinions regarding who is intended by it.

The first: that it is Abu Jahl and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Ad-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn Abbas. The second: Abu Jahl and Ammar ibn Yasir. Ikrimah said this. The third: Abu Jahl and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn as-Sa'ib and Muqatil said this. The fourth: Abu Jahl and Uthman ibn Affan. Ath-Tha'labi related it. The fifth: Abu Jahl and Hamzah. Al-Wahidi related it. The sixth: Abu Jahl and Umar ibn al-Khattab. The seventh: the disbeliever and the believer. Al-Mawardi related both.

(p-262) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do whatever you wish.﴾ Az-Zajjaj said: Its wording is that of a command, but its meaning is warning and threat.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾, meaning the Qur'an. Then He began describing the Reminder and left out the response to "inna" (indeed). Regarding its response here there are two opinions.

[One of them]: that it is ﴿Those are called from a distant place﴾, mentioned by al-Farra'.

The second: that it is omitted, and regarding its estimated form there are two opinions. One: "Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder, when it came to them, disbelieved in it." The second: "Indeed those who disbelieve will be recompensed for their disbelief."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is a Book, mighty﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions. The first: protected from Satan, so he cannot find a way to it; said by as-Suddi. The second: noble with Allah; said by Ibn as-Sa'ib. The third: protected from falsehood; said by Muqatil. The fourth: it is impossible for people to produce its like; related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Falsehood does not come to it﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: denial; said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: Satan. The third: alteration; these two were related from Mujahid. Qatadah said: Iblis cannot diminish from it any truth, nor add to it any falsehood. Mujahid said: nothing that is not part of it enters into it. Regarding His saying: ﴿from before it or behind it﴾ there are three opinions. The first: before its revelation and after its revelation. (p-262) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do whatever you wish.﴾ Az-Zajjaj said: Its wording is that of a command, but its meaning is warning and threat.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾, meaning the Qur'an. Then He began describing the Reminder and left out the response to "inna" (indeed). Regarding its response here there are two opinions.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 41, verses 43–44:

Allah's words: ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you.﴾ On this there are two views.

The first: it has been said about those sent before you that they were "a sorcerer," "a soothsayer," and "a madman," and they were denied just as you were denied. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, and the majority (al-Jumhur).

The second: "You are only told what the prophets before you were told, that Allah is Forgiving and that He is Possessor of severe punishment." This is related by al-Mawardi.

Allah's words: ﴿And if We had made it﴾, meaning the Book revealed to him, ﴿a non-Arabic Qur'an﴾, i.e., in other than the language of the Arabs, ﴿they would have said, "If only its verses had been explained in detail! Non-Arabic and Arab?!"﴾ i.e., why were its verses not made clear in Arabic so that we could understand it?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 41, verse 47–48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the Jews said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Tell us about the Hour, if you are a messenger as you claim." This was related by Muqatil. The meaning of the verse: none knows its establishment except Him, so when it is asked about, its knowledge is referred to Him.

(And no fruit comes forth from its sheath) Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "min thamaratin" (from a fruit). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "min thamarat" (from fruits), in the plural. ﴿From its sheaths﴾, i.e., its coverings (awi'yatiha). Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, from the places in which they were hidden. The sheath (ghilaf) of everything is its sleeve (kumm), and it is from this that the sleeve of a shirt (kumm al-qamis) is so called. Al-Zajjaj said: al-akmam (sheaths) are that which covers; every tree that brings forth something enclosed is "dhat akmam" (possessing sheaths). The sheaths of the palm tree are that which covers its heart (jimar) of palm fronds, fibre, and trunk; and everything the palm tree brings forth is "dhu akmam." So the spathe (talʿah) has its sleeve, which is its skin. From this, a skullcap is called kummah, because it covers the head; and from this are the two sleeves of a shirt, because they cover the two hands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the day He calls out to them﴾, i.e., God, exalted is He, calls out to the polytheists, ﴿"Where are My partners?"﴾ whom you used to claim. ﴿They will say, "We have informed You"﴾. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: we have informed You. Muqatil said: we have made You hear. ﴿None of us is a witness﴾. There are two opinions regarding this.

One: it is from the speech of the polytheists, and the meaning is: none of us is a witness that You have a partner; so on that day they will disavow what they used to say. This is the saying of Muqatil.

The second: it is from the speech of the deities that were worshipped, and the meaning is: none of us is a witness to what they said. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there will be lost to them﴾, i.e., there will be lost to them in the Hereafter, ﴿what they used to call upon﴾, i.e., worship in the world. ﴿And they will be certain﴾, i.e., they will be convinced, ﴿that there is for them no place of escape﴾. We have explained the word "mahis" (place of escape) in Surah an-Nisa' [4:121].

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 41, verses 49–52:**

(p-266) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: What is meant by "man" is the disbeliever. So the meaning is: the disbeliever does not grow weary of asking for good, ﴿from supplication for good﴾, that is, from his supplicating for good, which is wealth and well-being.

﴿But if evil touches him﴾, which is poverty and hardship, the meaning is: when he is tested with that, he despairs of the mercy of Allah and loses hope in His mercy. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-ya'us* is on the pattern *fa'ul* from *ya'isa* (to despair), and *al-qanut* is on the pattern *fa'ul* from *qanata* (to despair).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us﴾, that is, good, well-being and wealth, ﴿he will surely say: "This is mine"﴾, that is, "This is due to me for my deeds, and I deserve it." Then he doubts the Resurrection and says: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come﴾, that is, I am not certain of the resurrection. ﴿And even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him﴾, meaning Paradise, that is: just as He gave me in this world, He will give me in the Hereafter. ﴿Then We will surely inform those who disbelieved﴾, that is, We will surely inform them of the evil of their deeds.

As for what follows, it has already been mentioned (Ibrahim: 17; al-Isra': 83) up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and turns away, withdrawing to one side﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read *wa-na'a* (وَنَأى) like *na'a* (نَعى). Ibn 'Amir read *wa-na'a* (وَناءَ) with an open *nun*, lengthened, and the hamza after the alif. Hamza read *nini'a* (نِئِيَ) with a kasra on the *nun* and on the hamza.

﴿So he has long supplication﴾. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning of *'arid* (عَرِيضٍ) is "abundant." Whether you describe it as long or as wide, it is permissible in speech.

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to the people of Makkah: ﴿Have you considered: if it is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition﴾, that is, opposition to the truth, ﴿far away﴾ from it? The word *shiqaq* is a noun, and the meaning is: there is no one more astray than you. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of the verse is: "Then you disbelieve in it. Are you not in opposition to the truth and far from what is correct?" So the rest of the verse was placed in the position of this phrase.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 41, verse 53–54:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions.

The first: "in the horizons" means the conquest of the regions of the earth, and "within themselves" means the conquest of Makkah. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Suddi.

The second: that "in the horizons" refers to the events (waqai') of Allah among the earlier nations, and "within themselves" refers to the Day of Badr. This is the view of Qatadah and Muqatil.

The third: that "in the horizons" refers to the withholding of rain from the whole earth, and "within themselves" refers to the afflictions that occur in their bodies. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: that "in the horizons" refers to the signs of the sky, such as the sun, the moon, and the stars, and "within themselves" refers to (p-268) the occurrences on the earth. This is the view of Ibn Zayd. It is also reported from Ibn Zayd that what is "within themselves" is the path of excrement and urine, for a person eats and drinks from one place and expels from two places.

The fifth: that "in the horizons" refers to the traces of those disbelievers who passed away before them, and "within themselves" refers to their being created as a drop (nutfah), then a clot ('alaqah), then a lump of flesh (mudghah), then bones, until they were brought to reason and discernment. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾. Regarding the pronoun in "it" (ha' al-kinayah) there are two opinions. One: that it refers to the Qur'an. The second: that it refers to everything the Messenger called them to. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of the verse is: until they know the reality of what We sent down to Muhammad and revealed to him of the promise to him that We will make His religion prevail over all religions.

﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness?﴾ That is: Is it not sufficient for them that He is a witness over all things? Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Has not the testimony of your Lord sufficed them?

(p-269) The meaning of sufficiency here is: He has made clear to them what is sufficient as evidence for His Oneness and the confirmation of His messengers.

The first: "in the horizons" means the conquest of the regions of the earth, and "within themselves" means the conquest of Makkah. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Suddi.

The second: that "in the horizons" refers to the events (waqai') of Allah among the earlier nations, and "within themselves" refers to the Day of Badr. This is the view of Qatadah and Muqatil.

The third: that "in the horizons" refers to the withholding of rain from the whole earth, and "within themselves" refers to the afflictions that occur in their bodies. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: that "in the horizons" refers to the signs of the sky, such as the sun, the moon, and the stars, and "within themselves" refers to (p-268) the occurrences on the earth. This is the view of Ibn Zayd. It is also reported from Ibn Zayd that what is "within themselves" is the path of excrement and urine, for a person eats and drinks from one place and expels from two places.

The fifth: that "in the horizons" refers to the traces of those disbelievers who passed away before them, and "within themselves" refers to their being created as a drop (nutfah), then a clot ('alaqah), then a lump of flesh (mudghah), then bones, until they were brought to reason and discernment. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾. Regarding the pronoun in "it" (ha' al-kinayah) there are two opinions. One: that it refers to the Qur'an. The second: that it refers to everything the Messenger called them to. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of the verse is: until they know the reality of what We sent down to Muhammad and revealed to him of the promise to him that We will make His religion prevail over all religions.

﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is, over all things, a Witness?﴾ That is: Is it not sufficient for them that He is a witness over all things? Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Has not the testimony of your Lord sufficed them?

(p-269) The meaning of sufficiency here is: He has made clear to them what is sufficient as evidence for His Oneness and the confirmation of His messengers.
